items.title: Avery the Poké Kid’s Family Speaks Out After Scalpers Use Child’s Death to Inflate Card Prices
items.excerpt: The family of late Pokémon influencer Avery the Poké Kid is speaking out after scalpers have reportedly started using his death to artificially inflate the prices of a 30th Anniversary Jirachi SIR card.
items.content_text: The family of late Pokémon influencer Avery the Poké Kid is speaking out after scalpers have reportedly started using his death to artificially inflate the prices of a 30th Anniversary Jirachi SIR card. Avery the Poké Kid died at 12 years old after a seven-year-battle with pancreatic cancer in late September. He was a huge fan of the Pokémon franchise and its accompanying trading card game ; his parents had recorded the last time he opened a pair of card packs and shared the video to Instagram a couple days later, showing him excitedly pulling a 30th Anniversary Jirachi SIR card. The footage went viral within the Pokémon community and even caught the attention of the card’s artist , who tearfully reacted to the situation on social media — but now, scalpers are reportedly using the situation to their advantage. As pointed out by Dexerto , Pokémon TCG collectors have discovered that the 30th Anniversary Jirachi SIR card has started climbing in price, with one user on X/Twitter noting that it rose from $70 up to $100, most likely due to Avery’s viral posthumous video. The situation has sparked a wave of backlash within the TCG community, with one user writing on X, “So, what, we’re using a 12-year-old child’s death as a way to increase the price of a f**king Pokémon card? I’m utterly disgusted.” “I'm so glad I was able to get this card before these losers jack up the price. It would've been so much sweeter to make it so everyone could get it to remember him, but nothing matters more than money I guess…,” another remarked . The fervor around this particular card has grown so loud that Avery’s family is speaking out about the situation. They published a statement on Avery’s official Instagram account, where they distanced themselves from any cards supposedly being sold in his name and urged scalpers to take down any listings they may have that reference him. “We are not involved in or benefiting from any cards being sold in Avery’s name or likeness. We have not approved these sales. We have asked sellers to take their listings down. Please do so immediately. This does not honor Avery’s generous heart. We are mourning our son and caring for our children. Please let us do that in peace,” they wrote. Commenters are sharing words of support on the post and condemning the scalpers, with one writing, “I can’t believe scalpers are trying to profit off your pain. I’m so sorry, I can’t even imagine how this all is weighing on you guys when you’re just trying to live and heal.” “Horrible that you have to even talk about this. Just know that there are decent humans praying for your family and not involved with this,” another said. Scalpers haven’t been getting off scot-free, though; the Pokémon Company made enough supply for its 30th Anniversary collection that resellers felt the impact on their businesses and went viral after moaning about everyone else getting the chance to buy some stock for themselves at regular retail prices.

items.title: Microsoft Just Seemingly Killed Copilot+ Just 2 Years After Launch
items.excerpt: Microsoft debuted Copilot+ about two years ago in an effort to bring AI PCs to the mainstream. Now it seems like they're already going away.
items.content_text: Microsoft debuted Copilot+ about two years ago in an effort to bring AI PCs to the mainstream. Now, the company's most recent Surface devices have abandoned Copilot+. At the Qualcomm Summit in Hawaii, Microsoft debuted its new Surface Pro and Surface Laptop, both of which were mysteriously missing the Copilot+ branding. Microsoft Surface CVP Brett Ostrum told Windows Central when asked about the missing branding that, "These are not called Copilot+ PCs. They do meet all the requirements of our previous bar for what Copilot+ devices are." Those requirements revolve around an NPU (neural processing unit) with at least 45 TOPs of AI compute performance. Microsoft seems unwilling to share why it's ditching the Copilot+ branding, but the program has been divisive. When the first Copilot+ PCs rolled out, Microsoft had manufacturers change keyboard layouts to include a new Copilot key that'd bring up an AI chatbot. Windows 11 also had Copilot Recall added, which continuously takes screenshots on your PC, so that you can use AI to scrub back through them to help get work done in the future. Even though Microsoft seems to be abandoning the Copilot+ branding, the company is still very heavily in favor of AI. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella continues to obsess over AI and even tweeted earlier today that "we're building Copilot as a new OS for work that spans every model, every form factor, and every task." Microsoft's weird hardware initiative is gone, but the AI push is far from over. Luckily, it does seem like Xbox isn't being pushed too hard to broadly adopt AI. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma reassured gamers back in February that Microsoft won't force studios to use the technology. Although, Microsoft does continue to apply for patents that would use AI to show you ads in the middle of your games and even play your games for you.
items.title_en: Microsoft Just Seemingly Killed Copilot+ Just 2 Years After Launch

items.content_text: Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days doesn't kick off until October 6, but we're already seeing some early deals ahead of the two-day event, including a discount on one of my favourite razors. The Philips OneBlade Hybrid 360 is currently down to £34.99 at Amazon UK , giving you 36% off its £54.99 MSRP. It's not officially part of Prime Big Deal Days just yet, but with the main sale still a little way off, it's a decent early saving if you're in need of a new shaver and trimmer. If you're looking for a few extra attachments, there's also the set with 3X 360 Blades, 4X Stubble Comb (1,2,3,5mm), and 1x Body Kit down to £42.99 at Amazon right now as well. I've been using various OneBlade models for years, and wherever I've used them, they've generally done a great job. Facial hair, chest hair, the ol' back fluff - the OneBlade is surprisingly versatile. What I like most, though, is how comfortable the shave feels. I've used plenty of razors that leave my skin feeling itchy or looking a little blotchy afterwards, but I've found the OneBlade does a much better job of avoiding that. The 360 blade helps here, as it can flex to follow the contours of your face and reach those awkward spots, which for me is the bit underneath my jawline. This particular model comes with three blades, along with stubble combs that act as guards for 1mm, 2mm, 3mm and 5mm trims. There's also a 3mm body hair comb for taking care of, ahem, the less facial areas. We'll leave it at that. I'm also a fan of the battery life. As someone who shaves little and often, I don't find myself having to charge the OneBlade particularly frequently, with up to 45 minutes of shaving time per charge. When it does eventually run out, you can top it back up using the included USB-A cable. At £34.99, this is a decent saving on a razor I've personally got plenty of use out of. Just bear in mind that Prime Big Deal Days itself doesn't begin until October 6 , so if you're holding out for the main event, there's always a chance we'll see further discounts once the sale officially gets underway. items.title: We Build LEGO Mayor Manor: A Spooky, Not-So-Scary Halloween Build
items.excerpt: We build LEGO Mayor Manor, a new spooky-but-not-scary set that's perfect for Halloween season.
items.content_text: The new LEGO Midnight Valley Collection theme is the rough equivalent of the LEGO Winter Village Collection , only instead of centering around Christmas, this theme is based on Halloween. Assuming it follows the same trajectory as its predecessor, we'll likely see one major addition to this whimsical, haunted village each Autumn. The Mayor Manor, out now, is the theme's debut set ( see it at Amazon ). It's an engaging, enjoyable build, with a cool visual motif for LEGO to elaborate upon in the years to come. The Mayor Manor is not a "closed" building ; it is open in the back like a classic dollhouse, allowing the builder to observe and stage the interior to his or her liking. It comes in nine bags – paper rather than plastic, thanks to LEGO's ongoing sustainability initiative . The switchover has been gradual, starting in 2020 and ramping up considerably in the last two years or so. [A note about the paper bags: Make sure you shake and flatten them out completely before discarding them. Paper is not as slippery as plastic (nor as see-thru), and so if you're missing a piece, it might be stuck in the scraps. It happened to me twice during this build.] The design is very '90s Tim-Burton-meets-Addams-Family. You have traditional spires mixed with stained glass windows, along with a foreboding gargoyle perched on the roof. The tree leaves are off-color blue and green, which creates the impression that you're viewing this house in the twilight rather than the bright light of day. The house interior is well-appointed, featuring a fireplace which functionally connects to the house chimney on the exterior – a nice bit of logical, functional coherency. On the second floor, there's a grandfather clock with a golden pendulum and a face stuck at midnight. There's also a bookshelf, with the books inserted at various depths, which gives the space a bit of quirk and whimsy. If you enjoy putting together little builds, which you then insert, as furniture or other knick-knacks, into a larger build to create a whole? Then you'll really enjoy what's going on here. The designers draw a clear line of distinction between the facade of the house, versus the house itself . The house has structural integrity; it's a two-story, traditionally built structure with defined rooms, level floors, and straight lines. But the facade of the house – the way it presents itself externally – is skewed, as if it's actively falling apart. LEGO accomplishes this by clipping crooked walls and roofs onto the underlying building. It's a convincing visual effect that'll make you do a double take. Because half of the house appears destroyed and half appears relatively intact, we can imagine, in our mind's eye, how the house once appeared when it was whole. And it's especially cool to contrast that to the ruined state of the house, and see how this jagged split in the wall over here matches – like a high-concept jigsaw puzzle – to the broken wall over there. Have you ever seen Ripley's Believe it or Not! museums in tourist areas? They're these self-billed "Odditoriums" that capitalize, P.T. Barnum style, on the off-beat and strange: "Come see a real shrunken head!" "Gaze upon an Iron Maiden torture device from medieval times!" "Young lady, have you ever laid eyes on a two-headed goat?" I used to love these museums growing up, and I especially loved looking at their optical illusion facades from streetview, which made them appear as if they were sinking into the ground or experiencing the aftershocks of an earthquake. The closer I walked, the less convincing the illusion. But that also taught me something about myself – that knowing the 'trick' behind these illusions deepened my love for them rather than diminishing it. I thought about this while putting together the Mayor Manor, particularly its East Wing. LEGO tells a story through its presentation; a stubborn intrusive tree has grown into the house's foundations, and over time, it's punctured through the walls and wrapped itself around half of the second floor. It implies that the house is very, very old, but also that the inhabitants of the house – the pale-faced matron with the fur-lined shawl, and the maid and butler who wait upon her – are either indifferent to what's happening or are unable to prevent it. Are they ghosts or the undead? Were they once inhabitants of this house when they were alive? How long have they roamed these hallways in the years since? They don't look unhappy, strictly speaking. This sort of imaginative "what-if?" roleplay is essential, I think, to your full enjoyment of adult-geared sets like these. Because unlike many other 18+ sets, this is not a painstaking replica or a pop culture artifact; this is a playset, with the dimensions and features of one. Children have the ability to construct elaborate play scenarios—a skill we often lose as we grow older. LEGO sets like these give adults tacit permission to indulge in those joys once more. Children have the ability to construct elaborate play scenarios—a skill we often lose as we grow older. But even if you don't have the suspension of disbelief to throw yourself into fantasy entirely, there is still childish joy and escapism in imagining the inner lives of these minifigures, and in staging dramatic scenarios when putting them out for display. LEGO Mayor Manor, Set #11383, retails for $119.99, and it is composed of 1420 pieces. It is available for purchase now at Amazon and the LEGO Store .

items.title: Is Doctor Doom Putting Together a Team in Avengers: Doomsday?
items.excerpt: After seeing Avengers: Endgame Encore's new footage, we can't help but wonder -- is Doctor Doom putting together the Illuminati in Doomsday?
items.content_text: Face front, Marvel fans, because Avengers: Endgame – Encore is now in theaters. The limited rerelease of the Infinity Saga’s finale is actually quite a big event for the MCU, because it has additional footage for the IMAX and Infinity Vision versions of the film. We can also confirm that the leaked footage is indeed legitimate, with a new ending where Loki visits Steve Rogers and Peggy Carter, and additional post-credits scenes that connect to Avengers: Doomsday . But now that we’ve seen this new footage, has Marvel tipped their hand as to what Doctor Doom’s plan is in the next Avengers installment? Going by the scene where Doom kidnaps Bruce Banner, it appears that Doom may in fact be putting together his own team of heroes! How would this work? Let’s look at the comics and the implications of Encore’s additional footage to piece it together. Is the MCU Adapting Time Runs Out? Now that we’ve seen the extra scenes from Encore, it seems clearer than ever that the Russo Brothers turned to Jonathan Hickman’s run on New Avengers for inspiration when shaping Avengers: Doomsday. While we always knew that Secret Wars was coming, and that the film would most likely be based on the 2015 version of the event, adapting the events from Hickman’s Avengers run that led into that Secret Wars was not a guarantee. After all, the fifth Avengers movie was originally supposed to be The Kang Dynasty before Jonathan Majors was fired and the Multiverse Saga switched gears to feature Doctor Doom . Now that Doom is set in place, it makes sense to use more of Hickman’s material from New Avengers, which was a multi-year saga about a group of Marvel’s most intelligent heroes trying to prevent the death of the multiverse. If you aren’t familiar with the comics, here's a brief rundown. Hickman’s New Avengers actually starred the Illuminati — a team consisting of Iron Man, Mr. Fantastic, Black Panther, Namor, Doctor Strange, Beast, and Black Bolt. Together they worked in secret to stop the threat of the Incursions , which occur when Earths from two different realities collide, destroying both universes in the process. However, the book is far more depressing and tragic than most superhero fare, with the heroes betraying their morals and turning on each other as it becomes more and more apparent that no matter what they try, the death of the multiverse is inescapable. They even go so far as to destroy other Earths before they can collide with Earth-616, the primary Earth of Marvel comics, but it only delays the inevitable. The Doomsday trailers and new Encore footage point to the MCU giving us a live-action take on the Illuminati trying to prevent the collapse of the multiverse. This arc culminated in a story called Time Runs Out, where the Illuminati can no longer keep a lid on the multiversal collapse. Doctor Doom has been working on his own plan to destroy the Beyonders, who are responsible for the Incursions; he steals the Beyonders’ power, which he uses to create Battleworld from the shattered remnants of the remaining universes. He then remakes himself as God Emperor Doom and uses his cosmic powers to hold what is left of reality together. Fans of the comics will certainly want to see Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom ascend to God Emperor form in Secret Wars, but when it comes to Doomsday, the recent trailers and the new Encore footage point to the MCU giving us a live-action take on the Illuminati trying to prevent the collapse of the multiverse. Is Doctor Doom Going to Lead the Illuminati? Although we saw an alternate version of the Illuminati hailing from Earth-838 in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, the team hasn’t yet appeared in the mainline MCU. Conventional wisdom dictates that Doctor Doom would be the film’s main antagonist — the movie is called Doomsday after all — but what if the title has more than one meaning? Yes, the film features Doctor Doom, but could it not also mean that the end times are coming? That would certainly track with the new scene in Encore where the TVA find themselves scrambling as they monitor thousands of Incursions, with Ke Huy Quan’s Ouroboros saying that “the multiverse is collapsing.” Did the MCU’s Doctor Doom cause the Incursions, or is he actually trying to save what’s left of the multiverse? Going by the Doomsday footage, I’m inclined to say the latter. The TVA scene in Encore reveals that one of the worlds in danger is Earth-10005, aka the Fox X-Men reality. This tracks with a shot in the first Doomsday trailer where Patrick Stewart’s Professor X looks up to see another planet falling out of the sky. I’ve long theorized that the X-Men are doomed (!) in Avengers: Doomsday; Doom needing to destroy the Fox X-Men’s Earth to save another reality would be the perfect way to establish the movie’s stakes. Perhaps the scene from the trailer where Doom activates an army of Sentinels to fight the heroes isn’t the climactic finale, but actually a scene early on before Doom has managed to relay the gravity of the situation to everyone else. The Encore scene where Doom kidnaps Bruce Banner also supports this theory. In the comics, Bruce was a late addition to the Illuminati who the others didn’t want to have involved because of his past with the group — after all, they were the ones who shot him into space. But Banner is smart enough to figure out what's happening on his own, and joins the team midway through the story. While some may think the MCU’s Doom wants Banner for his gamma-powered alter ego, what if he actually wants Banner’s mind ? Is Bruce Banner the first recruit in Doom’s version of the Illuminati? Will Pedro Pascal’s Reed Richards have no choice but to join forces with his greatest enemy ? And what about the Latverian Witches whose costumes we saw at San Diego Comic-Con? Is that a pathway for Elizabeth Olsen's Scarlet Witch to finally return to the MCU as a member of Doom's team? Perhaps the plot of Doomsday is less about the heroes working together to confront Doom, and instead sees them divided over how to handle the threat of the Incursions. Maybe that’s the explanation for why Shang-Chi is fighting Gambit, or why Invisible Woman appears to be battling Namor. We won’t know for sure until Doomsday drops in December, but for now, the new teases from Encore are certainly tantalizing. What do you think will happen in Avengers: Doomsday? Let us know in the comments! Carlos Morales writes novels, articles, and Mass Effect essays. You can follow his fixations on Twitter .
items.title_en: Is Doctor Doom Putting Together a Team in Avengers: Doomsday?

items.title: LEGO Astro Bot Set Confirmed as Free Gift with Purchase of PlayStation
items.excerpt: LEGO has officially confirmed the rumors that it will offer an Astro Bot LEGO set as a free gift with purchase for early buyers of the LEGO PS1 set coming in October.
items.content_text: As is often the case in the world of LEGO, the rumors were true. A new listing shows that LEGO is giving away an Astro Bot set as a free “Gift With Purchase” to people who buy the upcoming LEGO PlayStation set when it goes on sale in October. LEGO Astro Bot is a 276-piece display set aimed at ages 18+ and will be unavailable to purchase separately. Pieces : 276 Ages : 18+ Set # : 40899 Release Date : October 1 for LEGO Insiders, October 4 for everyone The Astro Bot set features the boisterous, blue-and-white robot using its laser-induced hovering ability. Astro Bot has translucent blue beams emitting from its feet and is supported by a black stand that also features an Astro Bot logo sign. Despite being made of blocks, the PlayStation mascot looks just as rounded in LEGO form as it does in polygon form. At 276 pieces, it’s not a very large set, but it should look good displayed next to the LEGO PlayStation set it accompanies. Speaking of, LEGO PlayStation is a brick-built re-creation of the original PS1 console Sony first launched in Japan in 1994 . It’s not available for preorder, but it will be available to purchase on the LEGO Store when it releases on October 1 for anyone with a free LEGO Insiders account , or October 4 for everyone else. LEGO PlayStation is a near 1:1 scale model of Sony’s classic gray console and its first (stick-less) controller. It has “working” Power and Open buttons, and under the disc lid, you’ll find hidden dioramas of Ape Escape and Gran Turismo. A word of warning: if you want the best chance at getting the Astro Bot LEGO set as a Gift With Purchase , I’d highly recommend signing up for a free LEGO Insiders account and buying the LEGO PS1 set as soon as it goes on sale, typically at 12:01 a.m. local time the day it’s available – in this case October 1. Gifts with Purchase often run out of stock before the sets they accompany. And though they do occasionally come back later , you can’t count on it. For more, check out every announced LEGO set coming out in the future.

items.title: As Resident Evil Requiem Passes $500m Revenue, Analysis Shows 8.6% Sales Were on Xbox, With Remaining 91% Shared Between PS5 and Steam
items.excerpt: Resident Evil Requiem sold just 8.6% of its copies on Xbox, new sales analysis indicates.
items.content_text: Resident Evil Requiem sold just 8.6% of its copies on Xbox, new sales analysis indicates. Data published today by Alinea Analytics revealed the eye-opening split in platform sales for this year's brilliant Resident Evil game, offering yet another glimpse into Xbox's struggles against its rival, Sony's dominant PlayStation 5. Requiem is still selling faster than any other game in Capcom's survival horror series so far and has now passed $500 million in total revenue, with 8.5 million copies shifted across PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. But only 8.6% of that 8.5 million (around 731,000 copies) were sold for Xbox consoles. Compare that to the whopping 48.1% of copies sold on PS5 (around 4.01 million) and the relatively similar 43.4% of copies sold via Steam (around 3.69 million) and it's clear how far behind Xbox is here. On the one hand, this isn't a huge surprise. PS5 has sold well this console generation, with 95.3 million units shipped as of June. Six years into its lifecycle and with hardware prices on the rise, sales momentum has notably slowed. But the machine is guaranteed to get a shot in the arm this fall when GTA 6 arrives, and PS5 is exclusively plastered all over the game's marketing. Xbox Series X/S, on the other hand, has really struggled. Microsoft stopped reporting sales figures years ago, though its current pair of consoles are believed to have sold a little over 35 million units to date — a figure that's worryingly below the unpopular Xbox One, which shifted 58 million units during the last console generation. Today's data on Resident Evil Requiem sales comes just a day after report pointed to a similarly significant sales split for GTA 6 preorders. The Verge 's Tom Warren stated that pre-sales for Rockstar's upcoming blockbuster were "heavily skewed" towards PS5, something that had set off "alarm bells" within Microsoft's Redmond campus. In a statement shared with IGN , Xbox chief strategy office Matthew Ball responded to this claim by stating that, actually, Microsoft was "very happy with GTA 6 preorders," which were "breaking records for Xbox" and "matching our share of the console market." Exactly which records were being broken, though, Ball did not elaborate. Of course, no-one should expect a 50:50 sales split for Resident Evil Requiem or GTA 6 preorders across Sony and Microsoft's consoles. PS5 has clearly outsold Xbox Series X/S this generation by some margin, and no one at Xbox is trying to pretend otherwise. Still, what Ball appears to be suggesting — that GTA 6's pre-sales split simply represents the reality of the hardware situation — does not appear to hold up with Requiem sales, where Xbox can be seen lagging behind PS5 far more than its believed hardware sales might suggest. There's likely a number of reasons for this, and it's fair to suggest that Resident Evil is a long-lived franchise that has historically enjoyed more of a home on PlayStation consoles than Xbox, particularly in the series' homeland of Japan, where Xbox has never gained a proper sales foothold. But it's hard to look at just how far behind Requiem's Xbox sales split is and draw anything positive from it for Xbox. Are people who actually have an Xbox Series X/S now leaving it behind to play on PC or another console? Can these fans be tempted back next console generation, when Microsoft is believed to be launching a machine that can also play games from third-party PC storefronts? Whatever the case, this is another concerning sign as the company struggles through a huge reorganization aimed at ensuring its survival .

items.title: The Top 38 Best Simpsons Episodes
items.excerpt: Fire up the steamed hams. With The Simpsons returning for a 38th season, we look back at the show's most hilarious and enduring episodes.
items.content_text: With The Simpsons returning for an unprecedented 38th (!) season on September 27, we're once more looking back at the show's very best episodes. The Simpsons has been around for nearly four decades now, spawning over 800 episodes and one theatrical movie (Homer voice: one theatrical movie so far! ). It wasn't an easy task considering how many there were to choose from, but these 38 episodes (for 38 seasons) are essential viewing for anyone who enjoys hanging out in Springfield, USA. Even 38 episodes barely scratches the surface of what the show has given us over the years, of course. Let us know your picks for the best Simpsons episodes of all time in the comments section below. 38. The Springfield Files (Season 8) "The alien has a sweet, heavenly voice, like Urkel. And he appears every Friday night, like Urkel!" For some sitcoms, crossover episodes are an opportunity to generate buzz and gin up a few cheap laughs. But The Simpsons did something truly special when it crossed over with fellow Fox mainstay The X-Files. After a profoundly drunk Homer encounters what he believes to be an alien in the woods of Springfield, Special Agents Mulder and Scully pay a visit to investigate. Fittingly, both David Duchovny and Gillian Anderson stop by to voice their animated counterparts. What follows is a truly hilarious mash-up of two classic '90s shows with several of the show's most memorable gags. 37. The City of New York vs. Homer Simpson" (Season 9) "Of course you'll have a bad impression of New York if you only focus on the pimps and the C.H.U.D.'s." As time has worn on, we've increasingly seen the series rely on "The Simpsons are going to [insert global locale here]!" plots. As tired as that trope can be, it certainly worked wonders in the Season 9 premiere. Here, an ill-fated night of binge drinking forces Homer to travel to the one place on Earth he swore never to return - New York City. Watching Homer butt heads with an entire metropolis full of misanthropes and khlav kalash sellers never gets old. And it all pays off handsomely when Homer finally snaps and takes matters into his own hands. 36. "Bart Sells His Soul" (Season 7) "Come on, Milhouse, there's no such thing as a soul. It's just something they make up to scare kids, like the Boogeyman or Michael Jackson." "But every religion says there's a soul, Bart. Why would they lie? What would they have to gain?" Bart may be the designated troublemaker of the Simpson clan, but some of the series' most charming episodes explore what happens when he crosses a line and tries to find his way back to the light. For example, this classic and infinitely quotable gem from Season 7. After Bart befouls the church with rock and/or roll music, he winds up selling his soul to Milhouse and grappling with the ensuing existential crisis. It all wraps up with a wonderfully tender moment between Bart and Lisa and a reminder that Bart, for all his flaws, has a good heart. 35. “Homer the Great” (Season 6) "Why won't those stupid idiots let me in their crappy club for jerks?" "Homer the Great" is a classic, absurdist Simpsons episode of the type only the inimitable John Swartzwelder could write. When Homer discovers that Lenny and Carl are members of a secret society known as the Stonecutters, he winds up joining and bumbling his way into becoming their fabled Chosen One. Power goes to Homer's head, of course, and the ensuing rise and fall of Springfield's new god-king is a real hoot. Plus, this episode gets bonus points for its great use of guest star Patrick Stewart and having one of the show's catchiest original songs in "We Do." 34. “I Love Lisa” (Season 4) "Watch this, Lise. You can actually pinpoint the second when his heart rips in half." When it comes to all-time great Simpsons one-liners, it's impossible to top Ralph "Chicken Necks?" Wiggum. But every so often the series will make Ralph the main character rather than the dimwitted comic relief, and never more successfully than in this Season 4 gem. When Ralph is cruelly left out of the class' Valentine's Day festivities, Lisa takes pity on him and gives him a card. That, of course, immediately spirals out of control when Ralph decides that "I Choo-Choo-Choose You" means Lisa is madly in love. It's a sweet look at the pitfalls of young love, and a welcome reminder that Ralph can be a three-dimensional character... when he's not too busy gluing his head to his shoulder. 33. “Treehouse of Horror VI” (Season 7) "Lousy Smarch weather... 'Do not touch Willie.' Good advice!" Like the series as a whole, the annual Treehouse of Horror specials peaked fairly early on, back when the emphasis was more on spooky fun than parodying the hot movie franchises of the moment. The sixth special still ranks among the best of the bunch, particularly thanks to its hilarious slasher movie spoof "Nightmare on Evergreen Terrace." This is also the episode that gave us Homer Cubed, a then-groundbreaking segment that dragged Homer kicking and screaming into 3D. 32. “And Maggie Makes Three” (Season 6) "Aww... it's a boy. And what a boy!" "Uhh... that's the umbilical cord. It's a girl." Thanks to the perpetually sliding timeline of The Simpsons, the series has given us many conflicting accounts of what life was like when Homer and Marge were younger and learning the ropes of being parents. This episode ranks as the best of that particular formula. It springs from a simple question - "Why are there no baby pictures of Maggie in the house?" - and uses it as a springboard for a surprisingly heartfelt look at Maggie's origins and Homer's brief stint as a bowling alley employee. As cynical as The Simpsons can be, this episode truly wears its heart on its sleeve. 31. "Lisa the Iconoclast (Season 7) "Embiggens? I never heard that word before I moved to Springfield." "I don't know why. It's a perfectly cromulent word." In this episode, Lisa learned the same lesson Batman would come to understand in The Dark Knight - sometimes you need to let a city have its heroes, even if the reality doesn't actually measure up to the ideal. "Lisa the Iconoclast" is one of the stronger episodes to focus on Lisa's moral dilemma of the day. Here she makes it her mission to force Springfield to realize the truth about its beloved founder, Jebediah Springfield, only to once again find herself a town pariah. As with a lot of great Lisa-driven episodes, the focus is as much on Homer and the conflict between following his whims and wanting to live up to Lisa's expectations. A memorable guest performance from Donald Sutherland is the icing on the cake in this episode. 30. "One Fish, Two Fish, Blowfish, Blue Fish" (Season 2) "I want to share something with you - the three little sentences that will get you through life. Number one: 'Cover for me.' Number two: 'Oh, good idea, boss.' Number three: 'It was like that when I got here.'" While The Simpsons was still honing its voice in Season 2, this unusually dramatic episode offered a glimpse of the golden period that was to come for the series. Here Homer confronts his own mortality in a very real and immediate way, fearing he's just ingested a poisonous blowfish and has only one day left to live. The result could have been overly sentimental and melodramatic, but this episode toes the line between humor and tragedy easily enough. The scenes of Homer bidding farewell to his family and confronting his imminent demise show an unusually human side of a character who so often comes across as a self-centered, even sociopathic jerk. At the same time, this episode ends on an appropriately sly note. One minute, Homer is celebrating his second lease on life and promising to live every day to the fullest, the next he's stretched out on the couch with a half-eaten bag of pork rinds. 29. "Mother Simpson" (Season 7) "Alright! I admit it, I am the Lindbergh baby! Waah! Waah! Goo-goo! I miss my fly-fly, Dada!" "Are you trying to stall us, or are you just senile?" "A little from Column A, a little from Column B." While Abe Simpson is always a reliably entertaining supporting character, up to this point the show had never focused much attention on Homer's *other* parent. Who was Homer's mother, and what part did she play in raising this dysfunctional goofball? As "Mother Simpson" showed us, there's actually quite a story to be told there. This episode introduced fans to Moana Simpson (voiced by Glenn Close), Homer's long-lost mother who's spent the last several decades on the lam after running afoul of a (slightly) younger Mr. Burns. The ensuing family reunion is a lot of fun, from Homer's childish plays at attention to Lisa finally discovering a family member she can look up to. But ultimately, Moana realized she couldn't outrun her past, and that's where this episode finds its enduring appeal. Homer and Moana's tearful goodbye ranks among the most emotional moments of the show. It's basically The Simpsons' answer to Futurama's "The Luck of the Fryrish." 28. "King-Size Homer" (Season 7) "Your father can be surprisingly sensitive. Remember when I giggled at his Sherlock Holmes hat? He sulked for a week and then closed his detective agency." One of our favorite animated sitcom tropes is the episode where a character goes to extreme lengths to get out of having to perform an annoying task. "King-Size Homer" sees Homer transform into a 300-pound caricature of himself in order to get out of Mr. Burns' mandatory exercise program and enjoy the pleasures of working from home. But when nuclear meltdown looms, Homer has to race against the clock and his own, uncooperative body in order to save the day. "King-Size Homer" stands out for many reasons, whether because of its smartly crafted dialogue, the hilarious sight gag of Homer in a mumu or its effective blend of cynicism and sympathy regarding Homer's plight. 27. "Lisa's Wedding" (Season 6) "Oh-ho! An English boy, huh? You know, we saved your ass in World War II." "Yeah? Well, we saved your ass in World War III." Nothing illustrates just how ridiculous and unprecedented The Simpsons' multi-decade run is than episodes like "Lisa's Wedding." This episode flashes forward to what was then the far-flung, futuristic landscape of 2010 to explore what Springfield looks like 15 years in the future. Apart from the presence of Jetsons-style hover cars and Bart being gainfully employed, not much had changed. The 2010 humor alone would have been enough to make this episode succeed, but it also hinges on a romance between Lisa and her handsome, wealthy British suitor, Hugh (Mandy Patinkin). As much as Lisa may be embarrassed by her family, she can't bring herself to marry a man who won't accept them for who they are. Even though the whole future storyline is just a glorified "What if?" scenario, it serves as one of the more poignant looks at the love between Lisa and Homer. This would be the first of several times the show has looked into the future of the Simpson clan, but all others pale in comparison to "Lisa's Wedding." 26. "Who Shot Mr. Burns Parts 1 & 2" (Seasons 6 & 7) “Ever since the beginning of time, man has yearned to destroy the sun. I shall do the next best thing: block it out.” We're cheating a bit on this one by technically including two episodes, it's true. To date, "Who Shot Mr. Burns?" remains the only two-part storyline the show has ever tackled. And it was a gleeful parody of the infamous "Who Shot J.R.?" storyline on the 1980's soap opera Dallas. The first episode closed out Season 6, as Mr. Burns managed to piss off just about every resident of Springfield by stealing oil, blocking out the sun, firing Smithers and still, through it all, never remembering Homer's name. The episode ended on a cliffhanger, with Burns shot and dozens of Springfielders as potential culprits. Season 7 continued the drama as Chief Wiggum investigated the crime and Lisa raced to clear her father's name before he actually killed his boss. Both episodes were funny, certainly, but we also appreciate their darker edge and the whodunit mystery that kept Simpsons fanatics speculating and debating all through the summer of 1995. 25. "'Alone Again, Natura-diddly" (Season 11) "Now, now, now, don't beat yourself up. I'm the one who drove her out of her seat. I'm the one who provoked the lethal barrage of T-shirts. I'm the one who parked in the ambulance zone, preventing any possible resuscitation." Time all but stands still in Springfield, and no one ever actually ages on the show (not even little Maggie). So death is a topic that only comes up rarely. And rarer still does death strike a major recurring character. "Alone Again, Natura-Diddily" was motivated largely by the fact that Maude Flanders' voice actress had moved away from California, but the writers found a great storyline to explore in Maude's tragic, T-shirt cannon-induced death. This was the first major tragedy to strike the Flanders clan since Ned's brush with financial ruin in Season 1. It upset his comfortable, squeaky-clean world and allowed for an extended character arc to play out over the course of many seasons as Ned adjusted to the single-parent lifestyle and started dating again. It was one of several cases where a key twist has given an old character new life on this show. 24. Treehouse of Horror VII (Season 8) "Don't blame me, I voted for Kodos!" This is easily one of the best Treehouse of Horror installments we've ever gotten. And while both "The Thing and I" and "The Genesis Tub" are swell, it's really the third and final segment that steals the show here. "Citizen Kang" probably ranks as the single greatest Treehouse segment of all time. It may date back to the far-flung era of 1996, but "Citizen Kang" remains as politically insightful as anything The Simpsons has delivered over the years. It's also one of the most quotable Simpsons episodes ever. "Don't blame me, I voted for Kodos!" alone is one of the most iconic lines the show has ever produced. So go ahead, throw your vote away! 23. "Radioactive Man (Season 7) "My eyes! Ze goggles do nothing!" With "Radioactive Man," various characters learned that the glamorous allure of Hollywood doesn't always live up to reality. The episode saw a Hollywood studio choose Springfield as the location to shoot their big-budget Radioactive Man movie (starring Ranier Wolfcastle, of course). Bart's dreams of playing Fallout Boy were dashed when the role went to Milhouse. For his part, Milhouse wanted no part of the fame, fortune, and constant hassle that come with child stardom. Meanwhile, production ground to a halt as Mayor Quimby and the rest of Springfield bled the studio dry with bogus taxes and fees. In the end, nobody won, especially not Wolfcastle as he was swept away by a river of toxic waste. This episode was a great spoof of both Hollywood and superhero films, aiming its barbs at the Batman franchise in particular. 22. "Itchy & Scratchy Land" (Season 6) "We need more Bort license plates in the Gift Shop. Repeat, we are sold out of Bort license plates." How can you not love an episode that simultaneously parodies Westworld, Jurassic Park and the Walt Disney empire? This episode sees the Simpsons travel to the new Itchy & Scratchy theme park for their summer trip. And naturally, it's only a matter of time before Homer and Bart's promise not to embarrass Marge completely falls apart. Luckily, a little Chaos Theory causes an uprising of animatronic Itchy and Scratchy robots, providing for some much-needed family bonding. Anyone who has experienced the overwhelming assault of capitalism and corporate mascots that is Disney World can appreciate this episode. 21. "Lemon of Troy" (Season 6) "Homer, come quick! Bart's quit his tutoring job and joined the violence gang!" The Simpsons has always referenced an ongoing rivalry between Springfield and the neighboring city of Shelbyville. But it wasn't until "Lemon of Troy" that said rivalry truly took center stage. Here we saw Bart lead a crew of misfits (Milhouse, Nelson, Martin, etc.) on a quest to retrieve Springfield's beloved Lemon Tree from Shelbyville's miscreants. This in turn forced their parents to pile into Flanders' RV to rescue them. "Lemon of Troy" offered a fun glimpse into Shelbyville, which turned out to be an almost Mirror Universe version of Springfield in some ways. But the episode also hit all the right notes in terms of celebrating the peculiar sense of community among Springfielders and their mythologized town history. 20. "Homer's Enemy" (Season 8) "Yes, that's me, and the guy standing next to me is President Gerald Ford… And this is when I was on tour with the Smashing Pumpkins… Oh, and here's a picture of me in outer space." "You? Went into outer space? You?" "Sure. You've never been? Would you like to see my Grammy award?" As much as Homer is portrayed as an ordinary slob of a lower-middle class guy, he's had some pretty grand adventures and lucky breaks over the years. "Homer's Enemy" introduced us to Frank Grimes, the man who was everything Homer isn't. Grimes was intelligent and ambitious, yet he could never seem to catch a break in life. And all of his pent-up aggression burst forth when he encountered Homer, a happy family man with a house and a decent job and everything Grimes didn't have. Is it any wonder Grimey snapped? It was definitely amusing to see Grimey lash out at a man too happily obtuse to realize he had made a mortal enemy. But in some ways, this is one of the darker Simpsons episodes. It showed viewers that sometimes life really is unfair, and some people just don't get what they want out of life, no matter how hard they struggle. 19. "Homer vs. Lisa and the Eighth Commandment" (Season 2) "There's something wrong with that kid. She's so moral. Why can't she be more like...well, not like Bart..." Homer is a well-meaning guy, but sometimes his grasp of right and wrong is a little tenuous. And some of the most memorable conflicts on this show have come when the far more mature and morally pristine Lisa struggles to reconcile her beliefs with her father's actions. Case in point, this Season 2 episode where Homer became the most popular guy in town after getting an illegal cable TV hookup (this being a time when cable TV was still considered a luxury). Seeing her father so brazenly violate the Eighth Commandment caused Lisa no small amount of distress. The result was an endearing little drama as Homer struggled to live up to the man Lisa wanted him to be. It says a lot about Homer that he gave in and did the morally correct thing, not because he feared for his own soul, but because he didn't want Lisa to be unhappy. 18. "Bart the Lover" (Season 3) "Truly, yours is a butt that won't quit." Edna Krabappel's romantic misadventures have often been a focus of the series, as have her clashes with Bart, every teacher's worst nightmare. This episode combined both conflicts as it explored Edna's sad, lonely existence and the emergence of a bond between teacher and student. Bart pranked Mrs. K with a series of love letters inspired by his parents' own letters, only to feel a pang of regret when he realized the emotional damage he had caused. Luckily, it all worked out okay in the end. This episode also benefited from an amusing subplot involving Homer struggling to build a doghouse and accidentally teaching Todd Flanders how to swear. It had to happen sometime. 17. "Flaming Moes" (Season 3) "Moe, I haven't seen the place this crowded since the government cracked down on you for accepting food stamps." With as much alcohol as Homer consumes, it wasn't too surprising to learn in "Flaming Moe's" that he can mix a mean drink or two. Homer's bizarre creation, The Flaming Homer, brought a new level of success and prestige to Moe's Tavern. But leave it to Moe to hog all the credit and leave his friend and most loyal customer out in the cold. "Flaming Moe's" is just an all-around great episode, with a steady stream of gags and one-liners and some nice character gr…

items.title: Blizzard Dev Doubles Down on World of Warcraft Forever Being for Classic Players
items.excerpt: World of Warcraft Forever has already been massively successful, but it's widened the divide that's always been there between the Retail and Classic versions of the game. And, it seems like some of the folks at Blizzard are standing firm on one side of that line.
items.content_text: World of Warcraft Forever has already been massively successful , but it's widened the divide that's always been there between the Retail and Classic versions of the game. And, it seems like some of the folks at Blizzard are standing firm on one side of that line. Earlier this week, Blizzard world builder Matthew Armstrong discussed his mindset when building the world of Forever via a lengthy post on X/Twitter . "I am making WoW forever for the classic gamer," Armstrong began, "and for the millions of people who have had their accounts lapse over the years because they were not satisfied with changes that were made to the game." That stance isn't too surprising, earlier in the week another WoW Forever developer stood by Blizzard's decision not to include shared tagging as something "we simply must hold the line on." It sounds like Blizzard is trying its hardest to provide new content for Classic players without succumbing to the temptation of adding the modern quality-of-life features that some WoW players find so divisive. Armstong continued: "I could have taken it easy and just kept doing things like I had done for the past 8 years on retail... because I was much more familiar with it and it actually takes a lot less time to do (height maps on textures do a ton of heavy lifting). Because the reality is that the majority of retail players wouldn't care and would probably actually prefer it. But I felt I had a duty to uphold an artistic vision and integrity that millions of people expect from us." The reason this entire debate is even happening is because, of course, World of Warcraft Forever is the shiny new version of World of Warcraft and brings some improvements that Retail players would surely love in the modern version of the game. I for one, prefer retail for the more robust endgame pillars, but even I look at Forever's improved lighting, controller support, and Undead Paladins, and yearn for them in Midnight – even if the latter will be coming in the Eclipse update in patch 12.2. Forever is even getting heavy rain effects ! Of course, Armstrong's statement has sown some division among the WoW community. The responses to his post range from user MesciuSandman tagging Blizzard and asking "is it normal that one of your employees candidly states that the game that you are about to release was not created for a certain segment of your customer base?" Meanwhile BanKsEsports posted: "I just want to say THANK YOU. Jan 2021 was the last active sub I held, I had been playing constantly since day 1 release... then I just felt like it was an endless grind loop and too far away from something worth investing so much time into." This battle over the identity of WoW Forever is taking place during a beta where you can only play until level 20, mind you. Only a fraction of the content that'll be in the full game is available now, and we'll have to wait until November 4 to really see how the community will coalesce. In the meantime, Blizzard is trying to crack down on offensive character names , though it seems like some outright silly ones have been caught in the crossfire.

items.title: How One Crash Bandicoot Level Helped Build Naughty Dog
items.excerpt: From a quick-fix solution to a triple-A staple, this is how an early Crash Bandicoot level inspired decades of cinematic level design in Uncharted and beyond.
items.content_text: As Leon Kennedy, we fled from a giant, mechanical statue. Eleven years later, we guided Nathan Drake and his brother, Sam, as they escaped from relentless pursuers on a motorbike . And recently, we helped forge a path through a literal wave of plague-infested rats for A Plague Tale’s Amicia . Three examples from literally hundreds of cinematic chase sequences in video games that can all trace their roots back to an unlikely source. The colourful cartoon platformer that started it all: Crash Bandicoot . The running-towards-camera chase sequence is as popular now as it’s ever been, raising the cinematic tension in blockbuster games for the last 30 years. But its beginnings were humble, and its widespread use is all thanks to the Crash developers at Naughty Dog trying to solve a single problem: How do we show our character’s face more? From a quick-fix solution to a triple-A staple, this is how an early Crash Bandicoot level inspired decades of cinematic level design. Boulders is the fourth level in Crash Bandicoot, and takes the average player around 60 seconds to complete. Nestled amongst 31 other levels featuring lengthy side-scrolling gauntlets, tricky platforming, and painful difficulty spikes to overcome, it would be easy to assume that a quick, minute-long chase sequence wouldn’t be a particular highlight. But Boulders was the first of its kind. Any video game sequence where a character is chased towards the camera can trace its origins back to Crash Bandicoot. Perhaps the series it informed the most, though, was Naughty Dog’s own Uncharted series, which features multiple sequences of Nathan Drake running towards the camera across the entire series, as if it were a mandatory part of a Naughty Dog game’s DNA. Uncharted makes no secret of this fact. Long after Crash’s creators had left the company, Naughty Dog still paid homage to Boulders in Uncharted 4, when Nathan Drake was able to pick up the pad himself and experience the level firsthand. “It’s the modern Naughty Dog playing the antique Naughty Dog.” said Jason Rubin, a co-creator of Crash Bandicoot, in a 2019 interview with IGN . “What Nathan’s doesn’t understand is that this is basically the game that led to you. You exist because of this game!” The level design for Boulders began its journey in 1994. Naughty Dog, then a small independent studio fresh off the modestly performing Way of the Warrior, was ready to take the next step. And the soon-to-launch Sony PlayStation gave it a platform to try something no one had done before: create the first great 3D platformer. Super Mario 64 was still two years away and under lock and key, so the genre's rules were yet to be established by the king of platformers. Crash creators and Naughty Dog founders Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin saw an opportunity to stake their claim in the burgeoning genre. They immediately got to work, experimenting with how platforming could work in 3D, but they soon ran into an issue. The camera's always behind you. All you do is see Sonic's ass, but the front of the character is where the expression is. “We were trying to preserve all of the good elements of classic platform games,” explained Gavin in his 2016 blog post. “To maintain a solid control feel, we kept the camera relatively stable and oriented the control axis relative to the camera. This may seem obvious, but it wasn't at the time, and many 3D games used different (and usually inferior) schemes.” “What would it be really like to do a platformer in 3D?” Gavin later said in a 2020 interview with Ars Technica . “Imagine you're going through loops like in Sonic the Hedgehog, or you're jumping platforms or collecting stuff in 3D. The camera's always behind you. All you do is see Sonic's ass, but the front of the character is where the expression is.” Locking the camera behind the character is now a tried-and-true method, used in almost all third-person action games today. But Gavin and Rubin were concerned this perspective would limit the character’s ability to connect with players – a thought that was particularly troubling considering the technical hurdles the team had overcome to bring Crash’s expressions to life. “When Crash pulls his flat face out of the sand, shakes it off, looks confused, leaps up, looks at the camera and does his great big goofy smile… that sold Crash as a character,” explained Rubin. “No 2D game could afford the art, and no other 3D game had the facial animation that our system brought. And thus the main character transformed from an emotionless ‘vehicle’ to an emotive friend.” The team at Naughty Dog knew their character was something special, and his ability to emote and react like a Looney Tunes cartoon separated them not only from the current competition, but eventually even Super Mario 64, the competition they didn’t even know they had. For this advantage to work, though, they needed to find more ways to get Crash’s face front and center. “Our solution, which evolved over the next two years, was multi-fold,” shared Gavin in his blog post. “First, the character would start the game facing the screen. Second, we added 2D levels that guaranteed quality gameplay and a chance to see the character in a familiar pose, allowing comparison against old 2D games. And third, we would attempt the reverse of a Sonic ass level – the run INTO the screen.” A desire to show more of Crash’s face led the developers to make their first breakthrough into cinematic territory and, ultimately, create the blueprint for Crash Bandicoot’s most iconic perspective. The angle switch, though, led to another issue. In the “Sonic’s ass” levels, players were always presented with the oncoming threat on the horizon. Despite the level of challenge, the linear path always gave players the intel they needed to progress – ensuring that any failure was the fault of the player’s ability, rather than the game design. When you stripped that intel away, you lost a core fundamental of the design. Players were now running into the unknown, so the obstacle path had to be light and forgiving. Much like other 3D games of the era, where open spaces became detrimental to conflict, Crash’s front-facing levels had, through necessity, been stripped of any challenge or drama. Crash could not have succeeded without good gameplay. This was by far the hardest part of making Crash Bandicoot. “In 3D [platforming], you can just go to the right and avoid [enemies] entirely,” Gavin told Ars Technica. “You’ve added a whole dimension to the space, so now there’s too much empty space. It diluted the ratio between choice and conflict. We had to figure out how to compensate for this to maintain the action pace.” “With all our technical and art successes, the game could not have succeeded without good gameplay,” shares Rubin. “This was by far the hardest part of making Crash Bandicoot.” “We had this realisation that basically we had added a dimension, so the simplest strategy was to take out a dimension in some way,” said Gavin. “An example of that was the boulder level: the dimension we're actually taking out there is time.” The solution was to use time to dictate Crash’s running speed. To increase the tension, Crash could no longer leisurely navigate the path. Naughty Dog looked to cinema for inspiration, and settled on Indiana Jones’ iconic boulder escape as the device to help force the player into a time-pressured environment vital to maintaining the desired level of conflict “All this became the legendary boulder levels,” said Gavin in his blog post. “Apeing that moment from Raiders of the Lost Ark when the giant stone ball starts rolling toward Indy.” The combination of character and conflict gave birth to the Crash Bandicoot chase sequence. Its immediate success cemented the form as not only a Crash Bandicoot staple, but also the cinematic inspiration for both Naughty Dog titles and other developers’ action games for years to come. But Boulders' influence wasn’t limited to presentation. Crash Bandicoot arrived at the tail end of an era of punishing difficulty. In a time when arcade was king, most casual players couldn't finish a game, and game design often targeted difficulty to drive revenue. A failed run led to another coin in the slot, after all. But despite making sure Crash had its fair share of difficulty, Rubin and Gavin also wanted to create an approachable game – one that challenged skilled players but accommodated beginners and, perhaps more importantly, children. Eventually everyone succeeded at Crash. “We realised that if a novice player died a lot of times, we could give them an Aku Aku at the start of a round and they had a better chance to progress,” explained Rubin. “We also figured out that if you died a lot while running from the boulder, we could slow it down a little each time. If you died too much, a fruit crate would suddenly become a continue point. Eventually everyone succeeded at Crash.” It’s in this approach that you can see how, alongside scripted cinematic sequences, Crash Bandicoot also helped introduce another major video game design philosophy. Adaptive difficulty had been experimented with before, but in 1996, alongside the launch of Resident Evil, the background act of monitoring a player’s performance and adapting the game’s challenges to accommodate really began to take shape. The medium began to move away from punishing players for quarters to creating a dynamic experience that could tailor itself to your skill level. Crash Bandicoot was an overwhelming success on the PlayStation. The small team of developers managed to birth a PlayStation icon who’s still celebrated 30 years later, and laid the foundation for Naughty Dog to become the renowned, elite developer we know today. “I think we sold under 100,000 copies of Way of the Warrior, shared Rubin. “We sold 9 million copies of Crash.” “Crash Bandicoot was really the crucible in which the Naughty Dog philosophy was forged,” said Gavin. “We wanted to make a truly great game that was gonna be a classic, and to do that, we came to believe everything in it had to be great.” Naughty Dog exists today because of the risks taken on Crash Bandicoot. Their desire to show off impressive 3D facial animations led to a reinvention of platforming perspective, inspired a generation of chase sequences, and, perhaps most importantly, sparked Naughty Dog’s cinematic ambitions.
items.title_en: How One Crash Bandicoot Level Helped Build Naughty Dog

items.title: I Am Very Tired of Insomniac’s Approach to Marvel Supervillains
items.excerpt: I am very tired of Insomniac’s approach to Marvel supervillains, and it makes less sense than ever in Wolverine.
items.content_text: This is an IGN opinion piece from Carlos Morales. He’s read several thousand Marvel comics and gets annoyed when adaptations don’t feel true to the characters. Warning: this article contains spoilers for Marvel’s Wolverine. Marvel’s Wolverine is out in the wild, marking the fourth collaboration between Insomniac Games and Marvel. But instead of being a triumphant new entry in the studio’s catalog, Wolverine has had a shaky launch, scoring a 6/10 in IGN’s official review and being savaged by online commenters . While the game isn’t as bad as the worst of the backlash would have you believe – a 6 on the IGN scale means ‘okay’, after all – it doesn’t reach the heights of Insomniac’s best games. It also highlights one of the studio’s most frustrating trends endemic to its triple-A Marvel games: the way it adapts supervillains from the Marvel universe. All four of Insomniac’s Marvel games feature a story where the main villain is a close friend of the hero, and their falling out is the main source of the conflict. Not only is it unimaginative to keep recycling the same plot, but the recurring use of the trope has reached a new level of absurdity in Marvel’s Wolverine because it tries to tell that story with Mr. Sinister, one of Marvel’s most sociopathic antagonists. Let’s delve into why Insomniac needs a new approach to supervillains. We’re Friends, Bub Marvel’s Wolverine establishes an odd status quo for mutants in the world of Insomniac’s Marvel games. There are no X-Men, and Nathaniel Essex, who in the comics is traditionally the supervillain Mr. Sinister, has led the covert Team X for almost 30 years. The game opens with Essex meeting a feral Wolverine, and much of the game’s first half is spent elaborating on their shared history. Logan credits Essex with saving his life and giving him purpose, a role that in most other versions is played by Professor X. Fans of the source material figured that a twist revealing Essex’s true nature would come, and it certainly does, but the way the game executes that plot turn is muddied by how Essex is portrayed early on. Essex is not just Logan’s friend and commander of Team X. He’s also a mutant rights activist on a crusade to make the world safe for mutants by fighting Bolivar Trask and the Reavers. Although it’s later revealed that Essex lied about being a mutant and stole the X-gene from his wife Rebecca using mad science back in the 1800s, he still spends most of the game acting like a righteous champion of mutantkind. His plan to awaken dormant mutants using Sentinels powered by the Helix Engine (and killing any humans who happen to be in the way) feels like a scheme better suited to Magneto than Mr. Sinister. You could argue that this is a new take on Essex and shouldn’t be judged against his comic persona, but that idea falls apart when the game does have him take on his comic appearance and personality for the final level. He threatens global armageddon by unleashing a fleet of gigantic Helix Sentinels and wants to absorb all mutant X-genes into himself, but there’s no coherent development between his “I want to save mutantkind” and “I will kill everyone on Earth” mindsets. The beginning of the conflict between Logan and Essex also falls flat because it’s largely predicated on Essex being “too violent” in his methods before he turns into an omnicidal maniac at the very end. There’s a pivotal scene where Essex tortures Trask telekinetically despite Logan’s protests, so Logan mercy kills Trask to stop his suffering. This distinction in the degrees of violence feels arbitrary when Logan spends the whole game shredding hundreds if not thousands of people with his claws, often tearing his enemies apart in brutally painful ways. Was the reveal that Essex wiped Logan’s memories and reduced him to a feral state at the start of the game not enough to spark their divide? Weirdly, that’s one of the most on-brand moments for Essex despite the developers’ odd refusal to let him fully resemble his villainous alter ego. Sins of Sinister Insomniac’s attempt to create an emotional falling out storyline between Logan and Essex struggles because it requires turning Essex into a completely different character from his comic incarnation. If you’re not familiar with Mr. Sinister in the comics, he started as a scientist in the 19th century who became obsessed with eugenics and mutation. He was granted superpowers and immortality by fellow X-Men villain Apocalypse, and would later become one of the team’s greatest foes, as well as developing a special enmity with Cyclops and Jean Grey. Sinister has no illusions about the morality of his work; he calls himself Mr. Sinister , after all. He’s in it for science and satisfaction, and given all he’s done (including working with the Nazis in World War 2), there are few Marvel villains less suited to a more sympathetic portrayal. So while fans of the source material will likely find Essex being a mutant crusader confusing, newcomers to the character won’t understand why he goes full dark side at the end when he spends so much of the game touting the need to protect mutants. The game hints at a way to resolve this friction, but doesn’t actually make the connection: Apocalypse. The mutant megavillain is a major part of the game’s backstory, having turned Logan into his Horseman of Death many years ago. It’s even implied, but not stated, that Apocalypse gave Logan his adamantium skeleton instead of the Weapon X project. Apocalypse speaks to Logan in his mind multiple times, but doesn’t make a physical appearance aside from being in shadow in the post-credits scene. Since he’s an important (if unseen) part of Wolverine’s story, I can’t help but ask: why isn’t Apocalypse in league with Essex? It feels like Insomniac took Mr. Sinister and bent him out of shape to suit its story instead of writing a story that suited him. Although Sinister and Apocalypse have a long history in the comics, Essex in the game doesn’t seem to know who Apocalypse is, nor is it apparent that Apocalypse is influencing him from afar. Essex killing his wife to harvest her X-gene and psychically torturing Logan to remove his memories proves that Essex has been evil from the start, but if that’s the case, why was he acting like he was on the side of the angels for close to three decades? Why would he work so hard to show he cares about the welfare of mutants, to the point of trying to convince Logan of the righteousness of his actions even while laying siege to Madripoor? It almost feels like Essex is pursuing a greater goal that’s never made clear, but if Apocalypse was secretly ordering Essex to do all this, or if Essex knew of Apocalypse’s existence and was working against him by creating an army of mutants, a lot of Essex’s characterization starts to make more sense. Instead, we’re left with an unconvincing conflict between two “friends” that can’t land its emotional beats because there isn’t enough foundation to support it. On a more basic level, it’s also just not very fun to have a Mr. Sinister who doesn’t get to embrace the flamboyant villainy of his namesake. The game never even calls him Sinister – his name is always Essex in dialogue. Even the name on the health bar during his boss fight is Essex. It feels like Insomniac took Mr. Sinister and bent him out of shape to suit its story instead of writing a story that suited him. Sadly, this has been standard operating procedure for the studio for some time. Not So Bad Guys One of the reasons that Marvel’s Spider-Man is the best Marvel game ever made is that it told a surprisingly heartfelt story that flipped the typical Spider-Man and Doctor Octopus relationship on its head. In Insomniac’s universe, Otto Octavius started not as one of Peter Parker’s greatest enemies, but as his mentor, with Peter working on robotic prosthetics with Otto between superhero missions. The genuine bond between the pair was tragically corrupted by Otto’s desire for revenge against Norman Osborn and the psychological damage that using the tentacle apparatus did to his mind. It’s a very different take on the source material, but it works because it doesn’t fundamentally change who Doctor Octopus is. He’s always been a dark reflection of the man Peter could be if he took his academic gifts and used them for villainy instead of heroism. It also plays perfectly into Peter’s understandable desire for a father figure after the death of Uncle Ben, with Peter needing to accept that he has to make his own choices instead of emulating idols who can disappoint him. However, this alternate take on one of Marvel’s greatest villains had an unfortunate consequence: it worked so well that Insomniac has tried to replicate it in each subsequent game. The Tinkerer in Miles Morales, Venom in Spider-Man 2, and now Sinister in Wolverine are all former friends of each game’s protagonist, and all these stories are made worse by trying to redo what worked in the studio’s first Spider-Man. Phin Mason, aka the Tinkerer, is a supergenius friend of Miles who wants to attack the Roxxon Corporation, and falls into the all too common stereotype of leftist coded villains who have a “point” but are too cool with murder and therefore defined as evil by the plot. Her master plan to destroy Roxxon HQ puts all of Harlem in danger, and while the game tries to handwave this by saying she was unaware of the real blast radius because of a miscalculation, that’s an attempt to salvage her morals that also makes her look like an idiot. She also dies to get “redeemed,” which makes the whole arc feel pointless. Harry Osborn is turned into Venom in Spider-Man 2, and while Harry is not traditionally one of the hosts of the Venom symbiote, the idea was at least foreshadowed in the previous game because of the symbiote being inside of his recuperation chamber. Yet his transformation into Venom makes no sense. He wears the symbiote with no ill effects for a while before giving it to Peter, who immediately turns into a dick because of the suit’s influence, and when Harry gets the symbiote back he transforms into a monster who doesn’t share his motivations. Sure, Venom claims he wants to “heal the world” because that’s something Harry said before, but he’s actually trying to conquer the world with a symbiote army, and the final boss fight makes it clear that Harry is basically a prisoner of the suit instead of being responsible for his actions, rendering the supposed tragedy of the conflict inert. These diminishing returns hit a new low in Wolverine, where Essex doesn’t have a clear motivation for putting up a charade of heroism for so long. Essex acts heroic only so there can be a “twist” later on that he’s not, and the multitude of scenes where Logan and Essex yell at each other after the reveal don’t feel like former friends who can no longer see eye to eye so much as the script feeling obligated to have dialogue scenes between major action setpieces. By the time we get to the final boss fight, Essex is gleefully reciting cliché after cliché about “I am the future!” and “You have no chance!”, creating a climax that can be enjoyable as spectacle but is devoid of depth. It’s a sad state of affairs given how long the game was in development and how much the studio was clearly passionate about the property. This is not to say that future Insomniac Marvel collaborations are doomed, but if the studio wants to get back on top, it needs to take a hard look at its storytelling instincts. Hopefully by the time we get to Spider-Man 3, the Venom spin-off, or the X-Men game, Insomniac will learn that for supervillains, one size most definitely does not fit all. Carlos Morales writes novels, articles, and Mass Effect essays. You can follow his fixations on Twitter .
